title: Oncall sleuth: socket pinning & policy propagation diary
body:
Summary:

This is a working diary of the oncall sleuth for the 2026-04-27 incident where a subset of private/VPC control plane RPCs to customer firewalls started failing intermittently. Symptoms were: elevated control-plane RPC latency, tenant-traffic stalls for some sessions, and frequent socket close/open churn seen in the edge-proxy metrics. Impact: three customers reported degraded on-prem model serving (timeouts during model load), two had short (>30s) request tail latencies and then recovered. No data loss.

Why this doc exists: to capture live hypotheses, quick mitigations, temporary commands, and an early runbook sketch for handling similar socket pinning / policy propagation issues in Private/VPCs. This is explicitly not a final postmortem.

Timeline (high level, rough):
- 2026-04-27 03:07 UTC: Pager alert — control-plane RPC error rate > 1% on cluster vpc-us-west-2-kg1
- 03:09 UTC: Oncall stack assembled on #oncall-private; began simultaneous metric triage (prometheus + edge-proxy logs)
- 03:12 UTC: Observed increased TCP RSTs on egress to a small set of customer firewall IPs (pattern: connections terminated after ~95s)
- 03:20 UTC: Confirmed tenant-facing timeouts correlated to the same egress destinations; started temporary traffic steering to fallback-region (us-west-2-b)
- 03:35 UTC: Applied egress pinhole rule as emergency: allowed established sockets to keep NAT translations longer (temporary NAT timeout bump) — reduced new failures but did not eliminate
- 04:10 UTC: Hypothesis refined: interaction between our session reuse (socket pooling) and customer's firewall TCP session ageing triggers inconsistent packet acceptance (socket pinning mismatch)
- 05:00 UTC: Deployed a small proxy-side change disabling aggressive connection reuse for impacted tenants (config rollout 1%)
- 05:45 UTC: Observed marked reduction in RPC errors for impacted tenants; reverted 1% config to 100% rollout over next 40 minutes
- 07:10 UTC: Incident declared mitigated; follow-up action items created

Observations / evidence collected:
- Edge-proxy logs: repeated pattern "FIN, ACK" from firewalls followed by SYN retries from our side for previously established sessions.
- TCP dump (sample): many flows show out-of-order FIN -> SYN within NAT timeout window. Some clients (customer firewalls) are aggressively sending RSTs after a policy re-eval.
- Control-plane traces: requests that failed had identical upstream dest IP + port and showed long stall in SYN/handshake phase ~90s after initial connection (matches customer device session GC behavior)
- Metric spikes: conn_open / conn_close delta spiked on edge-proxy by 430% for tenants A and B.

Preliminary root-cause hypothesis (what we think happened):
A cascade of small config changes on a customer's firewall (policy reload) caused the firewall to aggressively tear down existing sessions (FIN/RST) while our connection pooling still believed sockets were healthy. Because we rely on NAT translations with relatively short timeouts in some on-prem topologies, reusing sockets led to packets being dropped and long retry/backoff behavior causing control-plane RPCs to fail. The control-plane then tried to route to alternate endpoints and some fallback logic introduced more connection churn, worsening the situation for a small set of tenants.

Why this hypothesis fits:
- The timing of failures aligns with firewall policy reload windows (customer confirmed a scheduled policy push at 02:58 UTC).
- Packet captures show active teardown rather than network-level blackhole (i.e., explicit FIN/RSTs).
- Temporary disabling of aggressive reuse reduced error rates, suggesting reuse + external teardown interaction.

Short-term mitigations performed (what helped):
- Traffic steering to fallback-region for affected tenants (reduced impact while we investigated)
- Increased NAT timeout on host-level (temporary config) for affected egress peers -> reduced premature NAT evaporation
- Temporarily disabled aggressive connection reuse on proxies for impacted tenants (config flag: proxy.conn_reuse.enabled=false) -> best immediate improvement
- Increased logging for conn lifecycle to correlate with customer policy events

Commands/snippets used (captured for runbook):
- Check active conn churn:
  sudo /opt/edge/bin/connstats --filter tenant=A --interval 60
  (looks for conn_open vs conn_close deltas)
- Dump packet capture for target IP
  sudo tcpdump -nni eth0 host 198.51.100.22 and tcp -w /tmp/fw-198.51.100.22.pcap
- One-off change to proxy config (hot reload):
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN' \n    https://proxy-control.internal/_admin/config \n    -d '{"proxy.conn_reuse.enabled": false, "filter.tenants": ["A","B"]}'
- Bump host NAT timeout (temporary kernel sysctl wrapper):
  echo 180 >/proc/sys/net/nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established
  # note: requires careful coordination with infra / capacity

Runbook sketch (early — to be cleaned up):
- Detection
  - Alert when conn_open/conn_close ratio > 3x baseline for > 2m for a tenant
  - Alert when control-plane RPC latency p50 -> p95 increases by > 2x and originates from same egress IPs
- Triage steps
  1) Identify tenants and egress peers with conn churn via connstats and flow logs
  2) Capture tcpdump for representative flows; check for FIN/RST vs blackhole
  3) Check customer change window (ask solutions-eng to confirm policy pushes)
  4) If FIN/RST pattern: consider temporary proxy.conn_reuse.enabled=false for impacted tenants
  5) If NAT expiration suspected and immediate fix needed: coordinate with infra to bump nf_conntrack timeout to 180s for impacted hosts
  6) If widespread and cannot mitigate: steer traffic to fallback-region or fallback-capacity (use console route override)
- Post-incident
  - Request customer's firewall vendor logs for policy push times + reason for session tears
  - Add customer-facing explanation & possible mitigation checklist to solutions-eng playbook

Open questions (to investigate during postmortem):
- What is the exact ordering between our connection reuse TTL and customer's session GC policy? Which side should be authoritative?
- Do certain firewall vendors send RSTs on policy reloads while others send FINs? (we saw variance between two customers)
- Is there a place to centralize per-tenant egress NAT heuristics so they adapt automatically to tenant-specific firewall behavior?

Follow-ups & action items (owners):
- (Arjun) Build a short-lived metric (conn_churn_index) and add an alert target -> PD-4315 (due 2026-05-07)
- (Gina) Draft customer comms template + solutions-eng checklist for on-prem policy reloads (due 2026-05-05)
- (Ethan) Prototype adaptive conn_reuse heuristic (disable reuse if churn > threshold) and small canary (due 2026-05-20)
- (Ravi) Research kernel-level NAT timeout defaults across our supported AMI images; propose safe default bump (due 2026-05-10)
- (Maya) Runbook cleanup and final postmortem draft (due 2026-05-12)

Notes / lessons learned (working):
- Our connection pooling assumption (long-lived sockets are always better) fails with aggressive third-party firewall policy reloads. We need to treat some tenants as having aggressive teardown semantics and adapt.
- Fallback routing is useful but adds operational complexity — better telemetry to detect early is preferable to mass steer.
- Conservative kernel-level NAT timeout bumps bring tradeoffs (conntrack table growth). Any host-level change needs capacity plan and can be tenant-targeted if we have a way to pinflows by tenant to host pools.

Appendix: raw excerpt from tcpdump (sanitized)

14:12:03.123456 IP 10.10.1.12.54321 > 198.51.100.22.443: Flags [S], seq 1000, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 123 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0
14:13:37.456789 IP 198.51.100.22.443 > 10.10.1.12.54321: Flags [R.], seq 3000, ack 1200, win 0, length 0
14:13:38.000112 IP 10.10.1.12.54321 > 198.51.100.22.443: Flags [S], seq 2000, win 64240, length 0

(we saw many such sequences where a previously established flow was RST'd, then our proxy retried with a new SYN; NAT mapping sometimes expired during retry causing blackhole symptoms)

Immediate recommendations (for runbook iteration):
- Add a per-tenant "egress-sensitivity" label; customers can opt into a safer connection profile (no pooling, longer NAT) during maintenance windows
- Implement an automated canary that flips proxy.conn_reuse=false for 1% tenants and monitors churn/latency changes over 24h
- Create a short KB for solutions-eng: "If customer performing firewall policy reloads, recommend hold on policy activation for 3 mins while connections quiesce OR coordinate times with Redwood oncall"

If you were oncall and found this doc: please add any missing commands, pasted logs, or conciliatory notes to the thread. I'll incorporate into the postmortem draft.

-- Maya
